title: Ken is the one thing the Barbie movie got right

commenti.body: [removed]
[removed]

Very astute analysis. I think you’ve shone a light on the key weakness of the narrative in this film, that Barbie hardly experiences the “real world.” Ken takes center stage, meanwhile Barbie’s exploration of Mattel headquarters is another fantasy land of tropes, an all male C-suite and the sage-ghost inventor herself tucked away carrying the true message of Barbie, if anyone will hear it.

The monologue was definitely a high point of writing in the film, and that it didn’t take an easy out is laudable for its honesty. I wish the film had spent more time with Barbie exploring the world. But overall I enjoyed it as a fun summer movie, but it’s not one I feel the need to revisit anytime soon.

I also want to say I appreciate the structure of your analysis. I found it easy to follow and I found myself nodding along.

>I think you’ve shone a light on the key weakness of the narrative in this film, that Barbie hardly experiences the “real world.” 

Yeah, it bothered me when I first saw it, and it was impossible to ignore on this rewatch: her experiences in the real world are mostly fantastical; they involve broad satire or the supernatural, and never build a solid foundation to justify her choice at the end.

>The monologue was definitely a high point of writing in the film, and that it didn’t take an easy out is laudable for its honesty. 

Funny you said it like this, because I got the feeling that this monologue was written and rewritten many times over - understandably! It's the moment where many of the movie's ideas are finally expressed out loud and it's palpable the filmmakers' worries to get it right. I dislike the overall context and how it influences the main Barbie's arc; I respect it for other reasons.

>I also want to say I appreciate the structure of your analysis. I found it easy to follow and I found myself nodding along.

Wow, thank you! :)

Exactly! The movie was never criticizing Mattel - at best, it was roasting the owners of its IP like Deadpool does with Marvel comics, minus the foul language; it's all harmless. Mattel's board is so outlandish that there's no way someone could ever interpret this depiction as anything resembling to the real institutional figures. Mattel's elevator replaces numbers with phrases such as "all the way to the top" or whatever. 

Mattel is as cartoonish as everything in Barbieland, which downplays the seriousness of any observation the film could have made about the financial aspects of the brand.

That’s the main thing that feels so off to me about the whole movie. You can do over the top campy comedy, and you can do biting satire. Some movies even manage to do both at once. I don’t think the satire part was done well, or at least not well-integrated with the humorous side.

My take is that the movie conveniently goes for broad satire to give an impression that’s leaving no stone unturned: they include Mattel in the story, which some saw it as a bold creative choice; by doing so, the movie implies that is not clueless about the commercial interests surrounding the character, but the “digs” at the company are all fair play and harmless. 

As in: Barbie’s creator is introduced as a ghost and comes back in the climax; the script throws in a joke about her criminal history (she was indeed charged with fraud in the 1970s, and somebody knew inquiring minds would bring this up if the movie never acknowledged it), and goes on to portray her ghost as this personification of human imagination and creativity.

IMO, the movie hides behind campy AND satire to get away with whatever it feels that it needed to cover - it's their excuse to say "don't take me so seriously"
True but the exec team is 5 men and one woman, and the woman is the HR officer.

I think your analysis of Ken is  spot on, but I have to disagree on Barbie. I don’t think the film hinges her entire development on the bench moment, the mean girls roasting, and the board. Those are just events that push her away from her initial refusal to accept complicated thoughts, but the real growth begins when she returns to Barbieland. Seeing how easily her friends fall into vapid, subservient roles shines a light on how superficial their previously dominant roles were. It unravels her corporate-approved “Girl Power” form of feminism by showing that without embracing the intellectual complexities of life, that type of feminism creates nothing lasting or stable.

America’s monologue on womanhood isn’t a revelation that woman don’t have it easy, it’s a revelation that allowing yourself to confront uncomfortable truths is what leads you to live a more thoughtful and meaningful life. (A revelation that is mirrored in the B plot with Ken.) And so by taking these difficult thoughts to her friends, she breaks through their haze of thoughtless existence and gives them the first tools to think critically. 

Barbie’s character at the beginning is purposefully simple, like a child playing at life with a dollhouse. It’s underdeveloped because she is underdeveloped, beholden to an allegorical role prescribed to her. To put it into the format you put forward:

What Barbie wants: To live a bubbly girl power existence free of any problems. 

What Barbie needs: To reckon with the complexities of both womanhood in particular and human existence in general so that whatever “power” or progress in life she gains is grounded in something real and meaningful. 

How Barbie gets from A to B: She starts having intrusive thoughts of mortality and finds it has something to do with a lack of belief by the girl playing with her in the real world. She finds this out from somebody who has physically been disfigured by her connection to the real world, foreshadowing that the road ahead will change her. 

Barbie then ventures to the real world where she starts to see her myth is utterly incongruous with the experiences of women: she is sexualized with an undertone of violence, she’s arrested for not understanding the rules of capitalism, the girls she thought she inspired reject her because she doesn’t represent their complex life experiences, and the corporation that glorified her now wants to literally imprison her in the role that serves them best. Mothers and daughters have conflict, youth isn’t a guarantee of happiness. But it’s not all bad. She also see glimmers of types of beauty that exist outside of her perfect girl power world: a beautiful old lady, people having a chill day in the park, the quiet calm of the little kitchen where her creator exists as a memory. When the choice to go back in her box comes, she rejects it and instead escapes back to her world to repair the gap between their mythological existence and the realities of everyday people. But upon her return she finds out that Ken brought the patriarchy back with him, and that her friends showed no resistance to it. 

All seems lost until she hears America Ferreira’s monologue and realizes that both she and her friends need to confront the world more mindfully, including uncomfortable truths. And in her accepting of that, she is able to do three things: use those uncomfortable ideas to weaponize the Kens’ sexism against them, share the ideas to “wake up” the other Barbies so they can critically assess their situation, and teach those Barbies how to share that knowledge and bring awareness to even more Barbies. In the end, OG Barbie not only has accepted the sort of complicated thought she initially rejected, but she’s used it to improve the meaningfulness of the lives of women and men in her world. She’s taught them to think critically so that they can live more authentically. 

With the success of this, she realizes for her life to have the most meaning she needs to give up her emotionally safe and physically immortal existence as an “idea” and live the short and complicated and sometimes mundane life of a real woman. This is represented beautifully in the final line of the movie. She goes from being the idea of a cis woman without any emotional or physical reality (she points out at the beginning she has no genitalia) to being very much real: she has genitalia that will need medical care, and she also now has the capacity for the emotional vulnerability of your first gynecological visit. 

I think the development of Barbie is more subtly done and difficult to pinpoint than that of Ken. It’s almost like she starts with a purposefully weak character and ends as a blank slate full of potential. But that journey from being an Allegory to being a Person was the most interesting part of the movie for me - a journey that mirrors one most people have as they enter adolescence and discover their individuality. Ken’s B plot refracted that journey in a more easily digestible way, which made the film all the more fun.

I thought it was a fun movie and a cool event, but I think any expectations that it would speak to real social truths are pretty misguided. At the end of the day it's a launch for a movie franchise about children's toys. Any filmmaker who makes a deal with the devil of these huge corporations are trading in their freedom to speak the truth.

I like Gerwig, but I don't think she's especially progressive or some champion for women, she has a safe, harmless, comfortably liberal perspective that doesn't really push any buttons. The way she centers Ken in the story says a lot.

Ken didn't explore much more, though, and they both spent enough time to get the core messages: for Ken, it's that the patriarchy let's men be powerful, and for Barbie, it was that the patriarchy does this at the expense of women's happiness and general safety. We got the scenes of her being scared and afraid, she didn't need to spend significantly more time there to drive the point home.

Imo, Barbie (the film)'s real problem was Barbie herself didn't *actually* have a clear arc. There are aspects of a "naive and shallow woman learns to confront the complexities of life" one, but the movie is very careful not to portray Barbies in Barbieland as *needing* to change, aside from how they don't take the Kens seriously. Unlike the other Barbies, though, who are smart and competent, *all* the Kens are himbos. There's Allen, but he's barely there.

Barbie learns the IRL patriarchy is scary and oppresses women, and she dismantles it when it comes to Barbieland by exploiting how the patriarchy also harms men. But she herself doesn't really learn or grow. Ken is the one with a very clear character arc.

Barbie could not have a fully rounded arc because the main point of the movie was to sell toys. We cannot feminist critique the brand we are selling in a meaningful way therefor it falls flat. However, I do not think Ken was super successful either. His misogyny is so childish that it feels more like a display of little boys than of adult men. Idk. I think this movie was fun but a huge mess.

Yeah I guess I disagree on this point. This is a stretch, but Barbie’s growth reminded me of Holly’s in The Third Man: she goes from a bit of an empty shell of a person floating through life, then transforms into somebody who makes the difficult choice because it’s the right one. Obviously two very different movies with two very different tones, but the sort of empty shell character start of Holly kept coming to mind for me. It was less about overturning the patriarchy and more about allowing womanhood to be defined independently, to balance community and expectations with the independence every human spirit has.

Ken didn't explore much more, though, and they both spent enough time to get the core messages: for Ken, it's that the patriarchy let's men be powerful, and for Barbie, it's that the patriarchy does this at the expense of women's happiness and general safety. We got the scenes of her being scared and afraid, she didn't need to spend significantly more time there to drive the point home.

Imo, Barbie (the film)'s real problem is that Barbie herself doesn't *actually* have a clear arc. There are aspects of a "naive and shallow woman learns to confront the complexities of life" one, but the movie is very careful not to portray Barbies in Barbieland as *needing* to change, aside from how they don't take the Kens seriously. Unlike the other Barbies, though, who are smart and competent, *all* of the Kens are himbos. Gosling Ken is one step away from an incel even before entering the real world, given his obsession with a woman who is clearly not interested. There's Alan, but he's barely there.

Barbie learns that the IRL patriarchy is scary and oppresses women, and she dismantles it when it comes to Barbieland by exploiting how it also harms men (and uplifting the other Barbies, though it's not like they were beaten down by the patriarchy before this). But she herself doesn't really change, and Barbieland is so different from IRL that it's hard to relate to her internal growth. Ken is the one with a very clear and relatable character arc.

Fun but a mess was essentially my immediate reaction and review on letterboxd. It had some genuinely hilarious parts and went by at a pretty brisk pace. But damn, the whole Mattel plotline was so cartoonish and half-baked it should have just been omitted. Barbie didn't have a lot to do despite Margot turning in a great performance. A lot of the framing/staging/cutting was also haphazard and amateurish. It just felt like a very all over the place movie that really kept the audience engaged with the performances and some clever dialogue.

Ken experiences the society from various men’s perspective on a montage “wide” level, Barbie experiences society on a personal level. She didn’t go around talking to executives or people at work, she got hit on by dudes walking by her and talked with girls and a mom off the clock. Ken doesn’t get to actually sit down and have a real conservation with a man who isn’t at work.

I feel the exact same way. If I didn’t watch it opening weekend with a packed and energetic theater, this movie would have faded from my mind already. They had some funny gags, a few good performances and a true vision when it came to barbieland’s set design, but everything felt slapdash.
I always go back to the awful Mattel boardroom scene and the awkward cut revealing America Ferrera’s eavesdropping. Like, Greta, I saw Little Women I know you’re better than this!

I don't see how we can possibly have serious feminist discourse about a film sponsored by mega-corporation Mattel that literally cost TWENTY DOLLARS TO WATCH AT HOME UNTIL LITERALLY YESTERDAY.

What a capitalist pseudo-intellectual storm of nonsense. Of course it's full of pandering in every direction and safely "centrist." 

I refuse to watch it unless someone I know has it for free or it comes to streaming.

Barbie is one big long pandering commercial. It is absolutely representative of bullshit, pop culture "white feminism" and anyone who doubts that needs to look no further than the fact that no one who wasn't willing to pay 25 dollars to sit in their own damn house and watch it couldn't for nearly six months.

It's a corporate dumpster fire.
It’s a shame because there are fun parts and Gerwig can direct and the actors could act, there was just 0 soul!

Every big blockbuster movie is sponsored by a mega corporation, only usually they're film studios. And like Mattel, film studios are responsible for their fair share of objectification of women. I don't care if you watch Barbie or not, but not watching Barbie because it is sponsored by Mattel is simply not a legitimate reasoning.

First of all, let me say I really enjoyed your analysis, and it gave me a lot to think about!

Here’s where I still disagree with you, and why I think that’s a major problem in the movie as a whole: America’s monologue on womanhood isn’t there just to empower OG Barbie, but every other Barbie as well. (It’s even a joke how she has to say it again and again to every other Barbies.)

The other Barbies have no idea how the real world works, because they were never in it. They go by what they are told: they first rule Barbieland because they believe women are the dominant gender in reality; they take subservient roles when Ken returns with his crazy ideas about the patriarchy; they understand, by America’s speech, that even though women still have it hard, there’s more to life than the hardships, and the challenges can make them even more resilient and creative and capable. 

I agree when you say that the speech addresses uncomfortable truths, but when it is repeated to the other Barbies, the endgame is to empower them and give them confidence to reclaim their place. We can argue that the monologue also inspired OG Barbie and, for her, it gave her enough confidence to make the decision to become human – a decision that was made because, since she experienced the real world firsthand, she wanted to use her newfound strength to make a real change. I don’t disagree with that.  

I just think this undermines the empowerment of the other Barbies that stay behind in fantasyland. Since they return to their original place in society, it’s almost like they’re getting a factory reset, not as if they’re fundamentally changed. Everyone in Barbieland goes by what someone tells them, by what they believe about a real world they never met for themselves – just like the society entirely changes when Ken brings his perspective, and changes yet again when America’s character shares her own, they still just go by what they’re led to believe.

You mentioned how the final line puts her in a physical reality by showing her first gynecological visit. I wonder if the focus on genitalia, in a movie that also presents a trans woman as one of the Barbies, is indeed a successful example emotional vulnerability (to me, it read like the punchline of a joke). I think this summons my impression of America’s speech: it’s a generic view on the female experience, and from a very Westernized perspective. If instead OG Barbie the movie had chosen a Black Barbie as its lead and taken her into the real world, she could experience harassment, but also racism; an overweight Barbie could experience different prejudices but maybe not the verbal harassment someone that looks like Margot Robbie would experience. 

Those are the kinds of uncomfortable truths that America’s “umbrella” monologue, and its broad feminism, could never be able to cover. Those are the kinds of uncomfortable truths that ignore complex and nuanced issues, which the movie, as a mainstream entertainment, never had any obligation to include. Yet the movie does feature this wide range of Barbies, but its big, turning-point speech, meant to empower these characters through uncomfortable truths, glosses over the challenges that many of those Barbies would face when existing as real women in the real world. That's why I said the movie treats them as secondary colors on its rainbow.

I never expected the movie to have serious feminist discourse. It's a mainstream movie with many financial interests behind it, so maybe the filmmakers pushed the message the farthest they could have under this circumstances. 

What bothers me, honestly, is how it made the most on the "appearance" of being daring, of addressing feminism, of addressing commercialism, of addressing inclusion. It was lauded as the first Barbie movie, but it's actually the first live-action that was theatrically released. 

Barbie has tons of movies released on video over the years; all of them feature the OG, stereotypical, white and blonde Barbie as the lead. This one presents a group of Barbies, yet the lead is the original model that looks like Margot Robbie; the other "diverse" Barbies serve no real purpose in the narrative. They being there makes the movie feel inclusive, makes Mattel feel like an inclusive company, and makes little girls everywhere feel like there's a Barbie that looks just like them in the stores to act as a conduit for their future dreams and ambitions.

Probably because somebody knew inquiring minds would wonder why the movie ignores such nuance, they decided to include Mattel on the plot; they couldn't paint the company in a bad light, so they resorted to broad satire - Mattel is as cartoonish as Barbieland, it conveys a stereotypical idea of patriarchy, and the financial interests are addressed in casual jokes that are ultimately harmless and never intended as a social commentary.

Yet the movie is very keen on the idea that girls all around the world can play with a Barbie that looks like them, that have their own house and hold high-profile jobs. It's eventually a message of inclusion by consumerism: you must have Barbie, and Barbie's house and everything else to be inspired to dream. If your parents can't afford a Barbie... let's not think about that.

First of all..

The set is probably as good as it could possibly be.

Second of all.. I have issues with the movie but I'm not sure they are common ones.

I think the subtext is that Barbie is cosmically linked to Gloria.

That's why she experiences the human emotions on her mind and body.

Gloria is in between drafts on a Barbie modification and MargotBarb experiences the physical consequences of those differing ideas. 

So stereotypical Barbie goes to the real world to try to help who she thinks is a problem child..

And then Ken comes along. 

I think it starts off on a good path with Barbie getting more insulted while Ken gets newfound respect that he never had in the Barbie world.

I do have an issue with Gloria's child calling SB fascist, simply because it kind of has vibe that she knows she's the real Barbie, but film mentions it twice at least that Sasha just think she's a crazy deluded character. 

So then the reveal happens pretty quickly that the distraught child is actually Gloria (actually I think that's really organic storytelling) 

So now that Ken is able to able to get a grasp of patriarchal rule due to his library comprehensive reading.

Now here's where I think it veers off..

Ken returns to BarbieLand to enact patriarchy. 

And to me, returning to Barbie land would be like Groundhog Day if Phil just found a secret door that would take him to a different day.

It's not that I want it to be impossible, but it shouldn't be an easy in. 

But the bigger picture is if Ken is no longer part of the real world, there are really no important consequences that can happen. 

The Barbie characters (including the Kens) are blank slates. If someone told them the world was flat, I'm sure there wouldn't be that much of an argument against it.

Not going to recap the plot because if you're on a thread you probably should have seen it. 

But what I will say that I think organic story would put a real world Ken against someone in the real world (I'll not lie and say Gloria isn't the character I am thinking of) and force Barbie to understand the problems of the real world but also understand the negative change in Ken himself.

Put everyone back in Barbieland and this complexity goes away.

This is just a bandwagon to the Mattel thing.

It would kind of be like if Marvel studios had a movie where the Disney got involved in the story, and was depicted as bumbling but innocent. 

I think it is kind of a corporate virtue signal, but I also think it's oddly sinister. "If I can show my top of the food chain company as being the type that would take five people to screw in a light bulb, I can attack my opponent in a far more brutal way."

But I think I'm really really overthinking this aspect.

Hey I'm not disagreeing..

But I think it makes sense that Ken is stunted because his whole world is essentially one where he competes with hunks to be recognized by Barbies.

Of course the whole movie is a toy commercial-- the funny parts is I think the least egregious moments are the ones where it kind of revels in its accessorized commercialism.
